title: The Silent Choke & Surgical Crisis
subtitle: Obstructive sleep apnea and sleep surgery
description: OSA screening, PSG severity grading, CPAP compliance, DISE-guided surgery, postoperative hemorrhage, and discharge wound care.

steps.title: Step 1/6: Clinical Symptoms and Screening
steps.scenario:
A 36-year-old man with a BMI of 26 kg/m² presents to your ENT clinic because of long-standing disruptive snoring.
His wife reports that his sleep has become increasingly abnormal.
On further questioning, he reports:
•	Excessive daytime sleepiness 
•	Nasal obstruction 
•	Sneezing 
His wife additionally reports recurrent pauses in breathing during sleep.
He has no known major cardiopulmonary or neurologic comorbidity.
Physical examination demonstrates:
•	Bilateral tonsils: Grade II 
•	Friedman tongue position: Class II 
•	BMI: 26 kg/m²
steps.media: Load image: SNOT-22, ESS, and STOP-Bang questionnaires
steps.question: Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: (A) Diagnose OSA clinically based on snoring and witnessed apnea alone.
(B) Use STOP-Bang as the definitive diagnostic test.
(C) Obtain objective sleep testing with polysomnography or an appropriate home sleep apnea test.
(D) Perform DISE before sleep testing to determine whether OSA is present.

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The combination of:
•	Habitual loud snoring 
•	Witnessed apnea 
•	Excessive daytime sleepiness 
creates a high clinical suspicion for OSA, but clinical history and screening questionnaires do not establish the diagnosis.
Objective sleep testing is required.
For an uncomplicated adult at increased risk for moderate-to-severe OSA, the AASM accepts either polysomnography (PSG) or a technically adequate home sleep apnea test (HSAT) as diagnostic options. 
Clinical Pearl: 
Screening estimates risk. Objective sleep testing establishes the diagnosis.
➡️ Transition
In this patient, an overnight PSG is obtained.
 
📚 Evidence
Kapur VK, Auckley DH, Chowdhuri S, et al. Clinical practice guideline for diagnostic testing for adult obstructive sleep apnea. J Clin Sleep Med. 2017;13(3):479–504. 
2026 note: AASM currently has a focused update of the adult diagnostic-testing guideline in development; the 2017 guideline remains the published diagnostic CPG at present.

steps.title: Step 2/6: PSG and Severity
steps.scenario: To confirm the diagnosis, you arrange overnight polysomnography. The report shows an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 33.7 events per hour.
steps.media: Load image: PSG tracing showing airflow cessation with oxygen desaturation
steps.question: Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: (A) The patient has moderate OSA, and the PSG identifies the tongue base as the major site of obstruction.
(B) The patient has severe OSA, but the AHI alone does not identify the anatomical level of upper-airway collapse or determine which operation should be performed.
(C) The patient has severe OSA, therefore tongue-base surgery is indicated

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

An AHI ≥30 events/hour is conventionally categorized as severe OSA.
Therefore:
AHI 33.7/h → Severe OSA
However, this is the first important surgical teaching point:
Severity ≠ Site of obstruction
PSG characterizes the physiologic burden of sleep-disordered breathing, but it does not tell the surgeon whether the dominant collapse occurs at the:
•	Velum 
•	Lateral pharyngeal wall 
•	Tongue base 
•	Epiglottis 
•	Or multiple levels 
The International Consensus Statement on OSA emphasizes that OSA evaluation and treatment require integration of sleep-study findings with the patient's phenotype and upper-airway anatomy. 
Clinical Pearl: 
AHI tells you how severe the disease is—not where to operate.

Transition: 
The patient now has an objective diagnosis: Severe obstructive sleep apnea
The next question becomes: How should he be treated initially?

Evidence
Chang JL, Goldberg AN, Alt JA, et al. International consensus statement on obstructive sleep apnea. Int Forum Allergy Rhinol. 2023;13(7):1061–1482.

steps.title: Step 3/6: Medical Management and Compliance
steps.scenario:
Because the patient has severe OSA with excessive daytime sleepiness, PAP therapy is recommended. He is started on nasal PAP therapy and receives treatment for his concomitant nasal symptoms.
However, despite attempts to use the device, he reports:
“I can't sleep with the mask on. I can't tolerate it.”
He requests a surgical option.
steps.question: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: (A) Discuss referral for comprehensive sleep-surgical evaluation and alternative treatment options.
(B) Proceed directly to UPPP because the tonsils are enlarged.
(C) Stop treatment because PAP intolerance means the OSA cannot be treated.

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

CPAP is strongly supported for adults with OSA and excessive sleepiness, and CPAP or APAP are standard ongoing PAP modalities. 
But if PAP is intolerable or unacceptable, the next step is not automatically a particular operation.
The AASM gives a strong recommendation that clinicians discuss referral to a sleep surgeon in adults with OSA who are intolerant or unaccepting of PAP; the guideline specifically supports this discussion for patients with BMI <40 kg/m². 
This patient:
BMI 26 + severe OSA + PAP intolerance
is therefore an appropriate candidate for surgical evaluation.
Clinical Pearl
PAP intolerance selects the surgical pathway. It does not select the operation.
Transition: 
Now that surgery is being considered, the surgeon needs to answer:
Where does this patient's airway actually collapse during sleep?

 Evidence
Patil SP, Ayappa IA, Caples SM, et al. Treatment of adult obstructive sleep apnea with positive airway pressure: An AASM clinical practice guideline. J Clin Sleep Med. 2019;15(2):335–343. 
Kent D, Stanley J, Aurora RN, et al. Referral of adults with obstructive sleep apnea for surgical consultation: An AASM clinical practice guideline. J Clin Sleep Med. 2021;17(12):2499–2505.

steps.title: Step 4/6: DISE and Surgical Intervention
steps.scenario:
Awake examination shows Grade II tonsils and Friedman tongue position class II.
However, the surgeon recognizes that awake anatomy may not reproduce the dynamic collapse that occurs during sleep.
The patient therefore undergoes:
Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy (DISE)
steps.media: Load image: DISE view showing soft-palate and tongue-base collapse during sleep
steps.question: Which anatomical level demonstrates clinically significant collapse （collapse > 50% of the original lumen）in this DISE video?

options.text: (A) Velum
(B) Oropharyngeal lateral walls
(C) Tongue base
(D) Epiglottis
(E) Arytenoid

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A,B,C

OSA is a dynamic upper-airway disorder.
DISE can reveal sleep-state collapse involving the:
•	Velum 
•	Lateral pharyngeal walls 
•	Tongue base 
•	Epiglottis 
and can demonstrate multilevel obstruction that may be incompletely predicted by awake examination.
AAO-HNS states that DISE may be useful in determining the most effective OSA surgical treatment plan. 
A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of DISE-guided upper-airway surgery also found that collapse patterns identified by DISE are associated with surgical outcomes and failure risk. 
 Clinical Pearl:
Awake examination describes anatomy. DISE demonstrates collapse.
Transition:
The airway assessment now suggests that the patient requires a site-directed multilevel surgical strategy.
The next decision is:
When should tongue-base surgery be added?
Evidence: 
AAO-HNS. Position statement: Treatment of obstructive sleep apnea. Revised 2021. 
Qi Y, Zhao Y, Yan Y, Wu D. Surgical failure guided by DISE in patients with obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2024;281(7):3333–3343.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Selecting the Operation
steps.scenario:
The surgical team plans treatment based on the patient's anatomical and dynamic airway assessment.
The final surgical plan includes: UPPP  + TORS tongue-base reduction
steps.media: Load image: Emergency endoscopic view showing a massive clot over the tongue base and tonsillar fossa
steps.question: Which finding provides the strongest rationale for adding TORS tongue-base reduction to the surgical plan?

options.text: (A) AHI >30 events/hour
(B) Clinically significant tongue-base / retrolingual obstruction demonstrated during airway evaluation in an appropriately selected patient.
(C) PAP intolerance alone

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

This is the central surgical principle of the case.
TORS is not an AHI-directed operation. It is a site-directed operation.
A patient can have an AHI of 50 without meaningful tongue-base collapse—and tongue-base reduction would not automatically be justified.
Conversely, when tongue-base obstruction is an important component of the patient's airway phenotype, TORS may be considered as part of an individualized surgical plan.
A 2026 systematic review of standalone TORS tongue-base surgery found that the published studies largely involved adults with:
•	Moderate-to-severe OSA 
•	PAP failure/intolerance 
•	Evidence of tongue-base hypertrophy/obstruction 
Mean AHI improved from 34.2 to 14.7 events/hour, but the authors stressed the limited number of studies, heterogeneity, and importance of careful patient selection. 
Why multilevel surgery?
If the patient has clinically important obstruction at both:
Palatal/pharyngeal level
and
Tongue-base level
then treatment may need to address both sites.
Clinical Pearl:
Multilevel surgery should be justified by multilevel obstruction—not simply by severe OSA.
The final question is:
How do you know whether the OSA was actually treated successfully?

 📚 Evidence
Chaidas K, Mouratidou S. Standalone transoral robotic surgery for obstructive sleep apnoea: A systematic literature review of clinical outcomes. Life. 2026;16(2):332. 
Mouratidou S, Chaidas K. Transoral robotic surgery for patients with obstructive sleep apnoea: A systematic review of current practices. 2024.
AAO-HNS recognizes tongue-base procedures, including midline glossectomy-type approaches, as potential components of comprehensive adult OSA surgical management.

steps.title: Step 6/6: Discharge Instructions and Wound Care
steps.scenario:
After appropriate postoperative healing, the patient reports:
“I feel much better, and my family says my snoring is much quieter.”
He asks:
“Does that mean my sleep apnea is cured?”
steps.question: What is the most appropriate method to determine whether surgical treatment has successfully controlled his OSA?

options.text: (A) Resolution of snoring alone
(B) Improvement in daytime sleepiness alone
(C) A wider airway on postoperative office endoscopy
(D) Clinical reassessment combined with objective follow-up sleep testing after an appropriate healing interval

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Subjective improvement matters, but:
Less snoring ≠ cure of OSA
and:
Improved ESS ≠ normalization of respiratory events
OSA treatment efficacy should include objective reassessment of sleep-disordered breathing after a non-PAP intervention such as upper-airway surgery.
Advanced Teaching Point
Sleep-surgery studies frequently use a criterion such as:
≥50% reduction in AHI + postoperative AHI <20
to define surgical success.
However:
Surgical success ≠ cure
A patient can meet a research definition of success and still have clinically important residual OSA.
Therefore outcome assessment should integrate:
•	Post-treatment AHI / REI 
•	Oxygenation 
•	Residual daytime symptoms 
•	Sleep-related quality of life 
•	Cardiometabolic context 
•	Need for adjunctive therapy 
Clinical Pearl: 
The operation is finished when the wound heals. OSA treatment is finished only when the outcome is objectively reassessed.
